question.text:
You are a portfolio manager provided with the expected return and standard deviation of four assets. Asset A: Expected Mean Return: 5%, Standard Deviation: 0; Asset B: Expected Mean Return: 10%, Standard Deviation: 10%; Asset C: Expected Mean Return: 12%, Standard Deviation: 15%; Asset D: Expected Mean Return: 7%, Standard Deviation: 17%.
Which of the three assets (B, C, or D) has the highest Sharpe Ratio?

explanation.text: The Logic: Sharpe Ratio = (Expected Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Standard Deviation. With Rf = 0%, Asset B = (10-0)/10 = 1.00, Asset C = (12-0)/15 = 0.80, Asset D = (7-0)/17 = 0.41. Asset B delivers the highest risk-adjusted return. The Trap: Picking C feels natural because 12% is the top absolute return, and 'B & C' tempts candidates who think high-return plus moderate-risk must tie. The trap is confusing absolute return with risk-adjusted return — Sharpe explicitly penalises every unit of standard deviation. Cross-Exam Context: Sharpe-based performance comparison is tested in NISM-Series-XV (Research Analyst), XXI-B (PMS Investment Adviser) and XIX-C/D/E (AIF Distributors / Managers). Distributor's Pro-Tip: Use the Sharpe Ratio — not the absolute CAGR — when a client asks 'why pay PMS fees when this mutual fund also did 12%?' A higher Sharpe quantifies how much of the return came from skill rather than from taking more risk.
